props.note: cited from the literature; the patent contests it for suitably reduced nickel
props.statement: The literature states that the presence of nickel or its compounds in a catalyst destroys or poisons it and tends to inhibit methanol formation; reduced nickel has been reported to react with carbon monoxide and the synthesis gas forming a volatile carbonyl compound which, it has been stated, inhibits the methanol reaction; by present theories nickel mainly causes methane and water.

props.statement: The lack of success of prior nickel catalysts is attributed to the character and degree of their activity: catalysts of high activity (nickel or nickel oxide with an inert support or another catalytic oxide) merely hydrogenated carbon monoxide completely to methane; ordinary nickel catalysts are, by the patentees' experiments, not suitable.

props.statement: Reduced nickel prepared by treating reducible nickel compounds (hydrate, oxide, nitrate, or organic salts such as oxalate or tartrate) with hydrogen at elevated temperature may form a very valuable methanol catalyst; any easily reducible nickel compound may be the base material.

lytic hydrogenation art that. nickel reduced.

props.note: stated as well established in the art, not as the patentees' own finding
props.statement: It is well established in the catalytic hydrogenation art that nickel reduced in admixture with an inert support is more active than the same compound reduced without a support at the same temperature, and that a reduction temperature above 300 °C gives a less active nickel catalyst than a lower one.

props.statement: There is probably an intermediate reaction in methanol synthesis, which may involve formaldehyde that is afterwards hydrogenated to methanol (CO + H2 = CH2O; CH2O + H2 = CH3OH); with carbon dioxide the first reaction is probably its reduction to carbon monoxide.

and no particle fusion is noted.

props.statement: Nickel reduced below 300 °C stays powdery without particle fusion and is so active that carbon oxides are completely hydrogenated; nickel reduced at 300-950 °C is apparently in a state of incipient fusion with just enough activity to stop at methanol; nickel reduced above 950 °C is, in the patentees' belief, so completely fused that its activity is destroyed.

props.method: precipitation of nickel hydroxide from a hot ~1% nickel nitrate solution with ammonium hydroxide; settling, decanting, centrifuging, washing, drying in 1 cm layers, breaking into granules
steps: a solution of nickel nitrate Ni(NO3)2.6H2O or similar soluble nickel salt is made up in distilled water to a concentration of about 1%
the solution is heated to 95-100° C. and treated with sufficient ammonium hydroxide to just render it alkaline, as indicated by 'brilliant yellow' indicator paper
the precipitate is allowed to settle and the supernatant liquor removed by siphoning or decantation
the precipitated nickel hydroxide is separated, e.g. by centrifuging, washed with about five times its volume of distilled water and separated again with a centrifuge
the moist precipitate is spread out on plates in layers about 1 cm in thickness and dried at 100-105° C. for about 10-15 hours
the hard dense cakes are broken up into granules of a size suitable for catalytic use
